sources: Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age, Nature Geoscience · Ulf Büntgen and others · 2016
f-536.text: A volcanic eruption, probably in Iceland, veiled the sky. Procopius said the sun shone 'like the moon'. Tree rings show the coldest decade in 2,000 years.
f-536.title: In 536 CE the sun went dim for eighteen months

sources: Pharos of Alexandria · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-alexandria-lighthouse.text: Built around 280 BCE and over 100 metres tall, it survived until earthquakes in the 1300s. Its stones were reused for a fort that stands on the site today.
f-alexandria-lighthouse.title: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood for over 1,500 years

sources: al-Khwarizmi · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-algorithm.text: Al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad around 820, was Latinised as Algoritmi. His book on equations, al-jabr, gave us 'algebra'.
f-algorithm.title: The word 'algorithm' is a mangled version of a Persian mathematician's name

sources: Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar, PNAS · Damian Evans and others · 2013
f-angkor.text: Lidar surveys in 2012 and 2015 revealed that Angkor spread over about 1,000 square kilometres with perhaps 750,000 people, hidden under forest because its houses were wooden.
f-angkor.title: The largest city of the Middle Ages was in the Cambodian jungle

sources: Decoding the Heavens · Jo Marchant · 2008
f-antikythera.text: The Antikythera mechanism, made around 150 to 100 BCE, used at least 30 gears to predict eclipses and track the Moon. Nothing as complex appears again for about a thousand years.
f-antikythera.title: The ancient Greeks built a computer out of bronze gears

sources: Digital Apollo · David A. Mindell · 2008
f-apollo-memory.text: Its software was woven by hand into magnetic cores. During the final descent it overloaded, shed low-priority tasks and kept flying.
f-apollo-memory.title: The computer that landed on the Moon had about 4 kilobytes of memory

sources: One Minute to Midnight · Michael Dobbs · 2008
f-arkhipov.text: On submarine B-59, cut off and under depth-charge attack during the Cuban Missile Crisis, Vasili Arkhipov refused to approve a nuclear torpedo launch.
f-arkhipov.title: One Soviet officer's 'no' may have prevented nuclear war in 1962

sources: The Adventures of Ibn Battuta · Ross E. Dunn · 1986
f-battuta.text: Ibn Battuta covered around 120,000 kilometres between 1325 and 1354, from West Africa to China, working as a judge for Muslim rulers along the way.
f-battuta.title: A 14th-century Moroccan travelled three times as far as Marco Polo

sources: Russia in the Age of Peter the Great · Lindsey Hughes · 1998
f-beard-tax.text: From 1698 bearded men had to carry a token proving they had paid. Nobles paid 60 rubles a year; peasants a kopeck at each city gate.
f-beard-tax.title: Peter the Great made Russian men pay a tax to keep their beards

sources: Report on the brewery accident, The Times · 1814
f-beer.text: A vat at the Horse Shoe Brewery ruptured on 17 October 1814, releasing over a million litres of porter into the slums of St Giles. Eight people died.
f-beer.title: In 1814 a flood of beer swept through a London street

sources: The Oxford Dictionary of Popes · J. N. D. Kelly · 1986
f-cadaver.text: Stephen VI had Formosus's body dressed in papal robes, tried, condemned, mutilated and thrown into the Tiber. Stephen himself was strangled within months.
f-cadaver.title: In 897 a pope dug up his predecessor's corpse and put it on trial

sources: Julian calendar · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-caesar-445.text: To realign the Roman calendar with the seasons, Julius Caesar inserted extra months. Romans called it the year of confusion.
f-caesar-445.title: The year 46 BCE lasted about 445 days

sources: Life of Caesar · Plutarch · 100
f-caesar-pirates.text: According to Plutarch, pirates captured the young Caesar around 75 BCE and demanded 20 talents. He insisted he was worth 50, paid, then returned with ships and had them executed.
f-caesar-pirates.title: Julius Caesar was kidnapped by pirates and complained his ransom was too low

sources: Cahokia Mounds · UNESCO World Heritage Centre
f-cahokia.text: Cahokia held perhaps 20,000 people and an earthen pyramid with a larger base than the Great Pyramid of Giza. It was abandoned by 1350.
f-cahokia.title: In 1100 the largest city north of Mexico was in Illinois

sources: The Lives of the Caesars: Caligula, 55 · Suetonius · 121
f-caligula.text: Suetonius says Caligula gave his horse Incitatus a marble stall and 'intended' to make him consul. Many historians read this as a joke mocking the Senate rather than a real plan.
f-caligula.title: Emperor Caligula supposedly planned to make his horse a consul

sources: The Sun Kings · Stuart Clark · 2007
f-carrington.text: The Carrington solar storm induced currents in the wires. Two operators in Boston and Portland disconnected their batteries and chatted for two hours anyway.
f-carrington.title: In 1859 telegraph operators sent messages powered only by the northern lights

sources: Pirates of the South China Coast · Dian H. Murray · 1987
f-ching-shih.text: Ching Shih commanded hundreds of ships in the South China Sea from 1807 to 1810, then negotiated amnesty and lived peacefully until 1844.
f-ching-shih.title: The most successful pirate in history was a woman who retired with a pardon

sources: Cleopatra · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-cleopatra.text: The Great Pyramid was finished around 2560 BCE. Cleopatra died in 30 BCE, roughly 2,500 years later. Apollo 11 landed in 1969, just under 2,000 years after her.
f-cleopatra.title: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid

sources: August Zang and the French Croissant · Jim Chevallier · 2009
f-croissant.text: Crescent rolls existed centuries before 1683, and the buttery croissant appeared in Paris in the 1830s. The legend dates from the 19th and 20th centuries.
f-croissant.title: The croissant was not invented to celebrate defeating the Ottomans at Vienna

sources: A Time to Dance, a Time to Die · John Waller · 2008
f-dancing.text: The 'dancing plague' began with one woman in July 1518 and spread to dozens, possibly hundreds. Mass psychogenic illness and ergot poisoning have been proposed; neither is proven.
f-dancing.title: In 1518 hundreds of people in Strasbourg danced for days, some until they collapsed

sources: Edge of Empires: A History of Georgia · Donald Rayfield · 2012
f-didgori.text: At Didgori in 1121, David the Builder's forces destroyed a Seljuk coalition in a narrow valley. Tbilisi was retaken the next year after nearly 400 years of Muslim rule.
f-didgori.title: Georgia's greatest victory was won by an army several times smaller than its enemy

sources: Dmanisi · Georgian National Museum
f-dmanisi.text: Fossils at Dmanisi date to about 1.8 million years ago. Their small brains overturned the idea that early humans needed big brains to leave Africa.
f-dmanisi.title: The oldest human remains outside Africa lie under a medieval Georgian town

sources: History of the Eiffel Tower · Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel
f-eiffel.text: It was built for the 1889 World's Fair with a 20-year permit and was due to be dismantled in 1909. Its value as a radio antenna saved it.
f-eiffel.title: The Eiffel Tower was originally meant to be temporary

sources: Parliamentary Debates (Hansard) · Parliament of Australia · 1932
f-emu.text: In 1932 soldiers with machine guns were sent to cull 20,000 emus in Western Australia. After a month, and fewer than a thousand birds, the operation was withdrawn.
f-emu.title: Australia once declared war on emus, and lost

sources: Alexander Bain · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-fax.text: Scottish inventor Alexander Bain patented an electric printing telegraph, the ancestor of the fax, in 1843. Bell's telephone patent came in 1876.
f-fax.title: The fax machine was patented before the telephone

sources: The birth of the Web · CERN
f-first-website.text: Tim Berners-Lee's page at CERN, describing the World Wide Web project, went live in 1991 and has been restored at its original address.
f-first-website.title: The first website is still online

sources: Inventing the Flat Earth · Jeffrey Burton Russell · 1991
f-flat-earth-myth.text: Educated Europeans had known the Earth was a sphere since the Greeks. Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Columbus popularised the myth.
f-flat-earth-myth.title: The idea that medieval people thought the Earth was flat was invented in the 1800s

sources: Geography, Book XI · Strabo · 20
f-fleece.text: Strabo wrote that people in Colchis, in western Georgia, caught river gold in sheepskins. The method was still used in Svaneti in the 20th century.
f-fleece.title: The Golden Fleece may have been a real gold-mining tool

sources: The Universal History of Numbers · Georges Ifrah · 1994
f-florence-ban.text: Authorities feared the new digits were easier to forge than Roman numerals written in words. Merchants kept using them anyway.
f-florence-ban.title: Florence banned Arabic numerals for bankers in 1299

sources: An Odd Kind of Fame: Stories of Phineas Gage · Malcolm Macmillan · 2000
f-gage.text: Phineas Gage lost his left eye and, his doctor said, much of his old personality. He later drove stagecoaches in Chile.
f-gage.title: A man survived an iron rod blasting through his skull in 1848 and kept working for years

sources: Murasaki Shikibu · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-genji-name.text: 'Murasaki Shikibu' is a nickname combining a character from The Tale of Genji with her father's court title. Her birth name was never recorded.
f-genji-name.title: We do not know the real name of the woman who wrote the world's first novel

sources: Living culture of three writing systems of the Georgian alphabet · UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage · 2016
f-georgian-alphabet.text: Its oldest inscriptions date to the 5th century CE. Three historical forms, Asomtavruli, Nuskhuri and Mkhedruli, are on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
f-georgian-alphabet.title: The Georgian alphabet is one of only fourteen scripts in the world in daily use

sources: Commentaries · Pope Pius II · 1460
f-glass-king.text: Charles VI suffered episodes from 1392 in which he refused to be touched and had iron rods sewn into his clothes so that he would not shatter.
f-glass-king.title: A king of France believed he was made of glass

sources: Göbekli Tepe · UNESCO World Heritage Centre
f-gobekli.text: Göbekli Tepe in Turkey dates to about 9500 BCE, before farming, pottery or metal. Its carved pillars weigh up to ten tons.
f-gobekli.title: Hunter-gatherers built stone temples 6,000 years before Stonehenge

sources: Ancient Wine: The Search for the Origins of Viniculture · Patrick E. McGovern · 2003
f-grape-varieties.text: That is more than any country of comparable size, supporting the view that the Caucasus was a centre of grape domestication.
f-grape-varieties.title: Georgia has over 500 native grape varieties

sources: By Permission of Heaven: The Story of the Great Fire of London · Adrian Tinniswood · 2003
f-great-fire.text: Only a handful of deaths were recorded in 1666. Historians suspect the true toll was higher, because the poor and the very old were rarely counted.
f-great-fire.title: The Great Fire of London destroyed 13,000 houses but officially killed only six people

sources: The Great Stink of London · Stephen Halliday · 1999
f-great-stink.text: In the hot summer of 1858 the sewage-choked Thames stank so badly that MPs funded London's modern sewers almost overnight after years of delay.
f-great-stink.title: A bad smell made the British Parliament pass a law in eighteen days

sources: Gregorian calendar · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-gregorian.text: Pope Gregory XIII fixed the drifting Julian calendar by ordering that 4 October be followed directly by 15 October. Protestant countries refused for up to 170 years.
f-gregorian.title: In October 1582 ten days simply did not exist

sources: Gutenberg: How One Man Remade the World with Words · John Man · 2002
f-gutenberg-sued.text: His investor Johann Fust sued for repayment in 1455 and won, taking the press, the type and the unsold Bibles.
f-gutenberg-sued.title: Gutenberg lost his printing press in a lawsuit the year his Bible was finished

sources: Hagia Sophia · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-hagia-sophia.text: Completed in 537 under Justinian, it held the record until Seville Cathedral in 1520. It has been a church, a mosque, a museum and a mosque again.
f-hagia-sophia.title: Hagia Sophia was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years

sources: Avengers of the New World · Laurent Dubois · 2004
f-haiti-debt.text: In 1825 France demanded 150 million francs to recognise the republic founded by former slaves. The debt, later reduced, took over a century to clear.
f-haiti-debt.title: Haiti paid France for its own freedom until 1947

sources: Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor · Martha T. Roth · 1997
f-hammurabi-beer.text: Law 108 of Hammurabi's code, around 1754 BCE, condemned a seller who overcharged or diluted drink to be thrown into the water.
f-hammurabi-beer.title: Babylon punished tavern keepers who watered down beer by drowning

sources: History of Rome, Book XXI · Livy · 10
f-hannibal-vinegar.text: Livy says the Carthaginians heated a rock blocking their path and poured vinegar on it to crack it. Polybius, the earlier source, does not mention it.
f-hannibal-vinegar.title: Hannibal's army may have split Alpine boulders with vinegar

sources: The Battle of Hastings 1066 · M. K. Lawson · 2003
f-hastings-arrow.text: A 1729 engraving shows the figure holding a spear. The earliest written account of Hastings says Harold was cut down by knights.
f-hastings-arrow.title: The arrow in King Harold's eye may have been added to the Bayeux Tapestry by 19th-century restorers

sources: Trepanation Procedures/Outcomes: Comparison of Prehistoric Peru with Other Ancient, Medieval, and American Civil War Cranial Surgery, World Neurosurgery · David S. Kushner and others · 2018
f-inca-surgery.text: Around 80 percent of Inca trepanation patients survived, judging by healed bone, against roughly 50 percent in the 1860s.
f-inca-surgery.title: Inca surgeons had better survival rates for skull surgery than American Civil War doctors

sources: Joan of Arc: A History · Helen Castor · 2014
f-joan-age.text: She lifted the siege of Orléans at seventeen in 1429, saw Charles VII crowned, and was executed at Rouen on 30 May 1431. A retrial in 1456 declared her innocent.
f-joan-age.title: Joan of Arc was about nineteen when she was burned

sources: Pure Ketchup: A History of America's National Condiment · Andrew F. Smith · 1996
f-ketchup.text: Ohio physician John Cook Bennett promoted tomato ketchup in 1834 as a cure for indigestion and other ailments. 'Tomato pills' were sold for years afterwards.
f-ketchup.title: In the 1830s ketchup was sold as medicine

sources: Signs of the Inka Khipu · Gary Urton · 2003
f-khipu.text: They recorded census, tribute and stores on knotted cords called khipu. Whether the knots also encode language is still unresolved.
f-khipu.title: The Inca ran an empire of millions without writing

sources: Jikji · UNESCO Memory of the World
f-korea-print.text: The Jikji, a Buddhist text, was printed with movable metal type in 1377. A copy survives in Paris.
f-korea-print.title: Korea printed books with metal type 78 years before Gutenberg

sources: Krakatoa: The Day the World Exploded · Simon Winchester · 2003
f-krakatoa.text: Krakatoa's 1883 explosion was logged as distant gunfire on the island of Rodrigues near Mauritius. Its pressure wave circled the Earth seven times.
f-krakatoa.title: The loudest sound in recorded history was heard 4,800 kilometres away

sources: Lincoln Cathedral · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-lincoln-spire.text: It lost the title only around 1311, when the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England reached about 160 metres.
f-lincoln-spire.title: The Great Pyramid was the tallest building on Earth for 3,800 years

sources: Louisiana Purchase · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-louisiana.text: Without the sugar colony, France had little use for its North American territory. The 1803 sale doubled the size of the United States for 15 million dollars.
f-louisiana.title: Losing Haiti led Napoleon to sell Louisiana to the United States

sources: Ada Lovelace · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-lovelace.text: Ada Lovelace published an algorithm for Babbage's unbuilt Analytical Engine in 1843. The machine was never completed.
f-lovelace.title: The first computer program was written a century before there was a computer to run it

sources: The First Voyage Around the World · Antonio Pigafetta · 1525
f-magellan-day.text: Sailing west with the sun, Magellan's survivors saw one fewer sunrise than people at home. Their careful log said Wednesday; it was Thursday.
f-magellan-day.title: The first crew to sail around the world came home a day behind everyone else

sources: Holocene dwarf mammoths from Wrangel Island, Nature · Sergey Vartanyan and others · 1993
f-mammoths.text: A small population of mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until around 2000 BCE. The Great Pyramid was completed around 2560 BCE.
f-mammoths.title: Woolly mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid was built

sources: Marathon · World Athletics
f-marathon-distance.text: The 1908 Olympic course was stretched to start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal family's seats. That odd distance became the standard in 1921.
f-marathon-distance.title: The marathon is 42.195 km because of a royal box in London

sources: Dark Tide: The Great Boston Molasses Flood of 1919 · Stephen Puleo · 2003
f-molasses.text: A storage tank holding about 8.7 million litres burst on 15 January 1919, sending a wave several metres high through the North End at around 55 km/h.
f-molasses.title: In 1919 a wave of molasses killed 21 people in Boston

sources: Becoming Mona Lisa · Donald Sassoon · 2001
f-mona-lisa.text: In 1911 Vincenzo Peruggia walked out of the Louvre with the painting. Two years of headlines and a sensational trial turned it into the most famous artwork on Earth.
f-mona-lisa.title: The Mona Lisa was not world-famous until someone stole it

sources: The Mongols and the Islamic World · Peter Jackson · 2017
f-mongol-post.text: The yam relay system placed horse stations every 30 to 50 kilometres across the empire. Riders carried a metal passport, the paiza, to demand fresh mounts.
f-mongol-post.title: A Mongol message could travel 300 kilometres in a day

sources: Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World · Jack Weatherford · 2004
f-mongol-tolerance.text: The Mongol Yassa guaranteed religious freedom across the empire, protecting Buddhist monks, Muslim imams, Christian priests and Daoist masters alike.
f-mongol-tolerance.title: Genghis Khan's law code exempted clergy of every religion from tax

sources: Company history · Nintendo Co., Ltd.
f-nintendo.text: Fusajiro Yamauchi founded Nintendo in Kyoto in September 1889 to make hanafuda playing cards. Its first video game came 86 years later.
f-nintendo.title: Nintendo was founded the same year the Eiffel Tower opened

sources: Njinga of Angola · Linda M. Heywood · 2017
f-nzinga.text: Offered only a floor mat in 1622, Nzinga of Ndongo refused the insult. She went on to fight the Portuguese for nearly forty years.
f-nzinga.title: An African queen sat on a kneeling servant to negotiate eye to eye with a Portuguese governor

sources: Olympic Games · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-olympics.text: From at least the 8th century BCE, athletes at Olympia competed nude. The Greek word gymnos, 'naked', is the root of 'gymnasium'.
f-olympics.title: Ancient Olympic athletes competed naked

sources: Ötzi the Iceman · South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology
f-otzi-tattoos.text: Ötzi the Iceman, found in Alpine ice in 1991, carries lines and crosses over his joints, placed where he had arthritis. Some researchers think they were a form of treatment.
f-otzi-tattoos.title: A 5,300-year-old man has 61 tattoos

sources: History of the University · University of Oxford
f-oxford.text: Teaching at Oxford is recorded from around 1096. The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, and the Aztec Triple Alliance that ruled the empire formed in 1428.
f-oxford.title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire

sources: Pantheon · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-pantheon.text: Rome's Pantheon, completed around 126 CE, spans 43 metres with no steel. Its concrete uses volcanic ash and self-healing lime.
f-pantheon.title: The world's largest unreinforced concrete dome is 1,900 years old

sources: The Diary of Samuel Pepys · Samuel Pepys · 1666
f-pepys-cheese.text: Pepys recorded burying his wine and cheese in the garden on 4 September 1666 as the flames approached. Parmesan was a luxury import.
f-pepys-cheese.title: During the Great Fire of London, Samuel Pepys buried his Parmesan cheese to save it

sources: The Pineapple: King of Fruits · Fran Beauman · 2005
f-pineapple.text: Pineapples grown in heated glasshouses were so expensive that hosts rented them as table decorations to impress guests, then returned them uneaten.
f-pineapple.title: In 18th-century Britain you could rent a pineapple for the evening

sources: Pompeii: The Life of a Roman Town · Mary Beard · 2008
f-pompeii-graffiti.text: The ash of 79 CE preserved everyday scribbles: election slogans, a weaver's love for a slave girl, and a customer's note that the innkeeper watered his wine.
f-pompeii-graffiti.title: Pompeii's walls carry over 11,000 pieces of graffiti, including love notes and complaints about bad wine

sources: Quarantine · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-quarantine.text: From 1377 Venetian territories held arriving ships offshore for quaranta giorni, forty days, to check for disease.
f-quarantine.title: The word 'quarantine' comes from the forty days Venice made ships wait during the plague

sources: Mémoires du général baron Thiébault · Paul Thiébault · 1893
f-rabbits.text: In July 1807 a hunt organised for the emperor used tame rabbits, which ran towards the hunters expecting food. Napoleon retreated to his carriage. The story comes from one general's memoirs.
f-rabbits.title: Napoleon was once chased off by an army of rabbits

sources: The Radium Girls · Kate Moore · 2016
f-radium.text: Women painting glow-in-the-dark watch dials pointed their brushes with their lips. Their employer knew radium was dangerous and did not tell them.
f-radium.title: Factory workers in the 1920s were taught to lick radioactive paintbrushes

sources: Roman road system · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-roman-roads.text: The empire laid about 80,000 kilometres of paved road. Layers of gravel, sand and fitted stone with a camber for drainage let many survive two millennia.
f-roman-roads.title: Roman roads were so well built that some are still driven on

sources: In the Devil's Snare · Mary Beth Norton · 2002
f-salem-hanged.text: English law treated witchcraft as a felony punishable by hanging. Nineteen were executed in 1692; one man was crushed under stones for refusing to plead.
f-salem-hanged.title: The Salem 'witches' were hanged, not burned

sources: Childbed Fever: A Scientific Biography of Ignaz Semmelweis · K. Codell Carter and Barbara Carter · 1994
f-semmelweis.text: Ignaz Semmelweis cut maternal deaths from about 18 to 1 percent in Vienna in 1847. Colleagues rejected the idea that doctors' hands carried disease.
f-semmelweis.title: The doctor who proved handwashing saved lives was driven out of medicine for saying so

sources: William Shakespeare · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-shakespeare-cervantes.text: Both died on 23 April 1616, but Spain used the Gregorian calendar and England the Julian, so Cervantes actually died ten days before Shakespeare.
f-shakespeare-cervantes.title: Shakespeare and Cervantes died on the same date but eleven days apart

sources: Anglo-Zanzibar War · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-shortest-war.text: On 27 August 1896 British warships bombarded the palace of Zanzibar. The sultan's forces surrendered after roughly 40 minutes.
f-shortest-war.title: The shortest war in history lasted less than an hour

sources: Gregorian Reform of the Calendar · G. V. Coyne and others (editors) · 1983
f-sweden-feb30.text: After botching a gradual switch of calendars, Sweden added a 30 February in 1712 to get back in step with the Julian calendar before adopting the Gregorian in 1753.
f-sweden-feb30.title: Sweden once had a 30th of February

sources: Native American gene flow into Polynesia predating Easter Island settlement, Nature · Alexander Ioannidis and others · 2020
f-sweet-potato.text: The sweet potato, a South American plant, grew across Polynesia before 1500, and Polynesian genomes carry Native American ancestry dated to about 1200 CE.
f-sweet-potato.title: Polynesians reached South America centuries before Europeans reached the Pacific

sources: Edge of Empires: A History of Georgia · Donald Rayfield · 2012
f-tamar-grave.text: Queen Tamar's grave was kept secret after her death in 1213 and has never been found. Gelati, Jerusalem and Vardzia have all been proposed.
f-tamar-grave.title: Nobody knows where Georgia's most famous queen is buried

sources: Tamar · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-tamar-king.text: Georgian reserves dedopali, queen, for a king's wife. Tamar, who ruled in her own right from 1184 to 1213, was called mepe, king.
f-tamar-king.title: Georgia's Queen Tamar held the title 'King of Kings'

sources: Tambora: The Eruption That Changed the World · Gillen D'Arcy Wood · 2014
f-tambora.text: The eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia in 1815 threw enough sulphur into the atmosphere to cool the planet. The next summer failed across Europe and North America.
f-tambora.title: In 1816 it snowed in June in New England

sources: Tbilisi · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-tbilisi-name.text: The Georgian word tbili means warm. Legend credits King Vakhtang Gorgasali with founding the city in the 5th century after a hunt led him to the sulphur springs.
f-tbilisi-name.title: Tbilisi is named after its hot springs

sources: Opium Wars · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-tea-britain.text: Tea imports drained British silver to China. Selling Indian opium reversed the flow, and when China tried to ban it, Britain went to war in 1839 and 1856.
f-tea-britain.title: Britain fought two wars to keep selling opium so it could afford Chinese tea

sources: Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés and the Fall of Old Mexico · Hugh Thomas · 1993
f-tenochtitlan-size.text: Tenochtitlan held perhaps 200,000 people in 1519, with canals, aqueducts and a market of 60,000 traders. Seville had about 60,000 inhabitants.
f-tenochtitlan-size.title: The Aztec capital was bigger than any city in Spain

sources: The Histories, Book VII · Herodotus · -430
f-thermopylae-shade.text: Herodotus attributes the line to Dieneces before Thermopylae in 480 BCE. Whether he said it or Herodotus polished it, it captured the Spartan style.
f-thermopylae-shade.title: Told Persian arrows would blot out the sun, a Spartan replied: 'Good, we'll fight in the shade.'

sources: The Bad-Ass Librarians of Timbuktu · Joshua Hammer · 2016
f-timbuktu-books.text: Family collections in the Malian city preserve texts on astronomy, law, medicine and poetry from the 13th century onward, many smuggled to safety in 2012.
f-timbuktu-books.title: Timbuktu's libraries hold hundreds of thousands of medieval manuscripts

sources: Paper and Printing, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 · Tsien Tsuen-hsuin · 1985
f-toilet-paper.text: The scholar Yan Zhitui wrote that he would not dare use paper bearing classical quotations for that purpose, showing the practice already existed.
f-toilet-paper.title: Toilet paper was in use in China by 589 CE

sources: Christmas Truce · Malcolm Brown and Shirley Seaton · 1984
f-truce.text: Spontaneous truces broke out along about two-thirds of the British front. Commanders forbade a repeat the following year.
f-truce.title: On Christmas 1914 enemy soldiers left their trenches to sing carols and swap gifts

sources: The meteoritic origin of Tutankhamun's iron dagger blade, Meteoritics & Planetary Science · Daniela Comelli and others · 2016
f-tut-meteorite.text: The iron blade's nickel and cobalt content matches meteoritic iron. In Bronze Age Egypt such iron was rarer than gold.
f-tut-meteorite.title: Tutankhamun was buried with a dagger made from a meteorite

sources: The World of the Fullo · Miko Flohr · 2013
f-urine.text: Roman laundries collected urine from street pots. As it ages it releases ammonia, which strips grease from wool. Emperor Vespasian even taxed the trade.
f-urine.title: Ancient Romans used urine to wash their clothes

sources: Vardzia · National Agency for Cultural Heritage Preservation of Georgia
f-vardzia.text: Vardzia, carved into the Erusheti mountain under Queen Tamar in the 1180s, held some 600 rooms, a church, wine cellars and irrigation, mostly hidden from invaders.
f-vardzia.title: A Georgian queen built a 13-storey city inside a cliff

sources: Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021, Nature · Margot Kuitems and others · 2021
f-vikings.text: Norse Greenlanders built a camp at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. Tree-ring dating shows they were cutting wood there in 1021 CE.
f-vikings.title: Vikings reached North America about 470 years before Columbus

sources: Early Neolithic wine of Georgia in the South Caucasus, PNAS · Patrick McGovern and others · 2017
f-wine.text: Residues of tartaric acid in Neolithic pottery from Gadachrili Gora date to about 6000 BCE. Georgians still ferment wine in buried clay qvevri.
f-wine.title: The oldest wine on Earth was made in Georgia 8,000 years ago

sources: Wojtek the Bear: Polish War Hero · Aileen Orr · 2010
f-wojtek.text: Wojtek was enlisted in 1944 so he could board a troopship to Italy. Soldiers reported he carried artillery shells at Monte Cassino.
f-wojtek.title: A bear served as a private in the Polish army

sources: Wu Zhao: China's Only Woman Emperor · N. Harry Rothschild · 2008
f-wu-characters.text: Wu Zetian, who ruled from 690 to 705, introduced about a dozen characters. 曌, combining sun, moon and sky, was hers.
f-wu-characters.title: China's only woman emperor invented new Chinese characters, including one for her own name

sources: Zero · Encyclopaedia Britannica
f-zero.text: A dot standing for zero appears in the Bakhshali manuscript, and Brahmagupta set out rules for arithmetic with zero in 628 CE. The idea reached Europe through Arabic mathematics.
f-zero.title: The number zero was invented in India

sources: Great Zimbabwe · Peter Garlake · 1973
f-zimbabwe.text: Archaeologists proved by 1905 that Africans built the medieval stone city. Rhodesia's white rulers promoted foreign-builder myths into the 1970s.
f-zimbabwe.title: A colonial government censored guidebooks to hide who built Great Zimbabwe

sources: Ada, Countess of Lovelace: Byron's Legitimate Daughter · Doris Langley Moore · 1977
Notes on the Analytical Engine, Scientific Memoirs vol. 3 · Ada Lovelace · 1843
Ada Lovelace · Encyclopaedia Britannica
ada-lovelace.text:
In 1843 a countess wrote an algorithm for a machine that would not be built for over a century

In 1843 Ada Lovelace published notes on Babbage's unbuilt Analytical Engine, including the first algorithm designed for a machine and the insight that computers could manipulate symbols beyond numbers.
ada-lovelace.title: The First Programmer Never Saw a Computer

sources: Agincourt: The King, the Campaign, the Battle · Juliet Barker · 2005
Agincourt: A New History · Anne Curry · 2005
Battle of Agincourt · Encyclopaedia Britannica
agincourt-1415.text:
A small, sick, exhausted English army beat a far larger French one

In 1415 a smaller English army won at Agincourt because mud, a narrow field and massed longbows neutralised French numbers.
agincourt-1415.title: The Battle Won by Mud

sources: Alexandria: Library of Dreams · Roger S. Bagnall · 2002
Libraries in the Ancient World · Lionel Casson · 2001
Library of Alexandria · Encyclopaedia Britannica
alexandria-library.text:
The Library of Alexandria was not destroyed in a single fire. Its end was slower and stranger

The Library of Alexandria declined over centuries through purges, wars and neglect; the single great fire is a later simplification.
alexandria-library.title: What Really Happened to the Library?

sources: Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar, PNAS · Damian Evans and others · 2013
Angkor · UNESCO World Heritage Centre
Angkor · Encyclopaedia Britannica
angkor.text:
Lasers flown over Cambodian forest revealed a medieval city the size of modern Los Angeles

Angkor, capital of the Khmer Empire, was a low-density city of perhaps 750,000 people around the temple of Angkor Wat; lidar surveys in 2012 and 2015 revealed its true size under the forest.
angkor.title: The Largest City of the Middle Ages Was in the Jungle

sources: Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism, Nature · Tony Freeth and others · 2006
Decoding the Heavens · Jo Marchant · 2008
Antikythera mechanism · Encyclopaedia Britannica
antikythera.text:
In 1901 divers found a lump of bronze in a shipwreck. It was a machine that predicted eclipses

The Antikythera mechanism, built around 150 to 100 BCE and found in 1901, is a geared astronomical calculator unmatched for a millennium.
antikythera.title: The 2,000-Year-Old Computer

sources: Digital Apollo: Human and Machine in Spaceflight · David A. Mindell · 2008
The Apollo Guidance Computer: Architecture and Operation · Frank O'Brien · 2010
Apollo 11 · NASA History Office
apollo-computer.text:
Apollo 11 landed with a computer weaker than a modern calculator, and it sounded alarms all the way down

Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969 guided by a 4-kilobyte computer with hand-woven memory whose priority-based software survived overload alarms during the final descent.
apollo-computer.title: The Computer That Landed on the Moon

sources: The Histories, Book VIII · Polybius · -140
Life of Marcellus · Plutarch · 100
Archimedes · Encyclopaedia Britannica
archimedes-syracuse.text:
Roman sailors grew so afraid of one old man's machines that they fled at the sight of a rope on the walls

Archimedes' catapults and ship-lifting cranes held Rome off Syracuse for two years until 212 BCE; the famous burning mirrors are a much later legend.
archimedes-syracuse.title: The Mathematician Who Held Off Rome

sources: The Submarines of October, National Security Archive Briefing Book 75 · Svetlana Savranskaya (editor) · 2002
One Minute to Midnight · Michael Dobbs · 2008
Vasili Arkhipov · Future of Life Institute
arkhipov-1962.text:
Two Soviet officers voted to fire a nuclear torpedo at an American carrier. The third vote was against

On 27 October 1962 Soviet officer Vasili Arkhipov refused to authorise a nuclear torpedo launch from submarine B-59 during the Cuban Missile Crisis, persuading the captain to surface instead.
arkhipov-1962.title: The Man Who Said No

sources: Russia in the Age of Peter the Great · Lindsey Hughes · 1998
Peter the Great: His Life and World · Robert K. Massie · 1980
Peter I · Encyclopaedia Britannica
beard-tax.text:
To modernise Russia, Peter the Great made men pay for their beards and carry a token to prove it

From 1698 Peter the Great taxed beards and issued tokens to payers as part of forcing Western customs on Russia's elite; the tax lasted until 1772.
beard-tax.title: The Tsar Who Taxed Beards

sources: The Black Death: A Personal History · John Hatcher · 2008
The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia, Nature · Maria Spyrou and others · 2022
Black Death · Encyclopaedia Britannica
black-death.text:
The deadliest pandemic in history killed a third of Europe, and the survivors got a pay rise

The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 killed a third or more of Europe; the resulting labour shortage doubled wages, weakened serfdom and reshaped the medieval economy.
black-death.title: The Plague That Raised Wages

sources: Antapodosis · Liutprand of Cremona · 960
The Oxford Dictionary of Popes · J. N. D. Kelly · 1986
Formosus · Encyclopaedia Britannica
cadaver-synod.text:
In 897 a dead pope was dug up, dressed in his robes, and tried in court

In January 897 Pope Stephen VI exhumed Pope Formosus, tried the corpse, mutilated it and threw it in the Tiber; Stephen was deposed and strangled within months.
cadaver-synod.title: The Pope Who Put a Corpse on Trial

sources: Natural History, Book XVIII · Pliny the Elder · 77
Calendar: Humanity's Epic Struggle to Determine a True and Accurate Year · David Ewing Duncan · 1998
Julian calendar · Encyclopaedia Britannica
caesar-calendar.text:
To fix the calendar, Julius Caesar made one year almost fifteen months long

In 46 BCE Julius Caesar, advised by the Egyptian-trained astronomer Sosigenes, stretched one year to about 445 days and introduced the 365-day calendar with a leap day.
caesar-calendar.title: The Year That Lasted 445 Days

sources: Cahokia: Ancient America's Great City on the Mississippi · Timothy R. Pauketat · 2009
Cahokia Mounds · UNESCO World Heritage Centre
Cahokia Mounds · Encyclopaedia Britannica
cahokia.text:
In 1100 the largest city north of Mexico stood by the Mississippi. Its main pyramid is still there

Cahokia, built around 1050 near the Mississippi, was the largest city north of Mexico with earthen pyramids and perhaps 20,000 people; it was abandoned by 1350.
cahokia.title: The American City Bigger Than London

sources: Paper and Printing, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 · Tsien Tsuen-hsuin · 1985
Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu) · Fan Ye · 445
Cai Lun · Encyclopaedia Britannica
cai-lun-paper.text:
Europe needed another thousand years to learn what a Chinese eunuch showed his emperor in 105 CE

In 105 CE Cai Lun presented an improved paper made from bark, hemp and rags to the Han court; the technology took a thousand years to reach Europe via the Silk Road.
cai-lun-paper.title: The Court Official Who Invented Paper

sources: The Sun Kings: The Unexpected Tragedy of Richard Carrington · Stuart Clark · 2007
Solar Storm Risk to the North American Electric Grid · Lloyd's of London · 2013
Carrington Event · NASA Science
carrington-1859.text:
In 1859 auroras reached Cuba, and telegraphs kept working with the power switched off

The Carrington Event of September 1859, the first observed solar flare, caused worldwide auroras and sparking telegraphs; a repeat today could cripple power grids and satellites.
carrington-1859.title: The Day the Sun Set Telegraphs on Fire

sources: Pirates of the South China Coast, 1790–1810 · Dian H. Murray · 1987
History of the Pirates Who Infested the China Sea from 1807 to 1810 · Yuan Yonglun, translated by Karl Friedrich Neumann · 1831
Zheng Yi Sao · Encyclopaedia Britannica
ching-shih.text:
She commanded more ships than most navies and beat the Chinese, British and Portuguese fleets

From 1807 to 1810 Ching Shih commanded the largest pirate fleet in history in the South China Sea, defeated every navy sent against her, and negotiated a full pardon that let her retire wealthy.
ching-shih.title: The Pirate Queen Who Retired Rich

sources: Christmas Truce: The Western Front, December 1914 · Malcolm Brown and Shirley Seaton · 1984
Silent Night: The Story of the World War I Christmas Truce · Stanley Weintraub · 2001
Christmas Truce · Encyclopaedia Britannica
christmas-truce.text:
On Christmas Eve 1914 enemy soldiers climbed out of their trenches, shook hands and exchanged buttons

On Christmas 1914 about two-thirds of the British front and their German opponents held spontaneous local truces, exchanging gifts and burying the dead; commanders ensured it never happened on that scale again.
christmas-truce.title: The Night the Guns Fell Silent

sources: Life of Antony · Plutarch · 100
Cleopatra: A Life · Stacy Schiff · 2010
Cleopatra · Encyclopaedia Britannica
cleopatra-moon.text:
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid

Cleopatra, who died in 30 BCE, lived about 2,500 years after the Great Pyramid but under 2,000 years before the Moon landing.
cleopatra-moon.title: Cleopatra and the Moon Landing

sources: Inventing the Flat Earth: Columbus and Modern Historians · Jeffrey Burton Russell · 1991
Admiral of the Ocean Sea · Samuel Eliot Morison · 1942
Christopher Columbus · Encyclopaedia Britannica
columbus-flat-earth.text:
Columbus was not brave for sailing off a flat Earth. He was wrong about how big the round one was

Columbus's 1492 voyage was opposed not because scholars thought the Earth flat but because they correctly judged Asia too distant; the flat-Earth story was invented in the 19th century.
columbus-flat-earth.title: Nobody Thought the Earth Was Flat

sources: 1453: The Holy War for Constantinople · Roger Crowley · 2005
The Fall of Constantinople 1453 · Steven Runciman · 1965
Fall of Constantinople · Encyclopaedia Britannica
constantinople-1453.text:
A city that had resisted sieges for a thousand years fell in 53 days

In 1453 Ottoman cannon ended a thousand years of Constantinople's invincibility, closing the Byzantine Empire and opening the age of gunpowder warfare.
constantinople-1453.title: The Walls That Finally Fell

sources: A Time to Dance, a Time to Die: The Extraordinary Story of the Dancing Plague of 1518 · John Waller · 2008
In a spin: the mysterious dancing epidemic of 1518, Endeavour · John Waller · 2008
Dancing plague of 1518 · Encyclopaedia Britannica
dancing-plague.text:
In July 1518 a woman began dancing in a Strasbourg street. Within a month, hundreds had joined her

In July 1518 hundreds of people in Strasbourg danced uncontrollably for weeks, some to death; the leading explanation is mass psychogenic illness driven by fear of Saint Vitus's curse.
dancing-plague.title: The Town That Could Not Stop Dancing

sources: The Life of King of Kings David · Anonymous Georgian chronicler · 1130
The Making of the Georgian Nation · Ronald Grigor Suny · 1994
Edge of Empires: A History of Georgia · Donald Rayfield · 2012
didgori-1121.text:
A king sent 200 riders to 'surrender', and they cut down the enemy's commanders instead

At Didgori on 12 August 1121, David IV's Georgian army destroyed a much larger Seljuk coalition in a narrow valley; Tbilisi was retaken the next year and Georgia's golden age began.
didgori-1121.title: The Day Georgia Turned the Tide

sources: A Complete Skull from Dmanisi, Georgia, and the Evolutionary Biology of Early Homo, Science · David Lordkipanidze and others · 2013
Earliest Pleistocene Hominid Cranial Remains from Dmanisi, Republic of Georgia, Science · Leo Gabunia and others · 2000
Dmanisi · Georgian National Museum
dmanisi.text:
The oldest human remains found outside Africa, 1.8 million years old, lie under a Georgian town

Dmanisi in Georgia holds the oldest human fossils outside Africa, about 1.8 million years old; their small brains and simple tools overturned assumptions about what early humans needed to leave Africa.
dmanisi.title: The First Europeans Were Georgian

sources: History of the Eiffel Tower · Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel
Eiffel Tower · Encyclopaedia Britannica
La Tour de Monsieur Eiffel · Bertrand Lemoine · 1989
eiffel-temporary.text:
The Eiffel Tower was supposed to be torn down after 20 years

The Eiffel Tower, built for the 1889 fair with a 20-year permit, survived because it became an indispensable radio antenna.
eiffel-temporary.title: The Tower That Was Meant to Disappear

sources: Parliamentary Debates (Hansard), House of Representatives, 8 November 1932 · Parliament of Australia · 1932
Coverage of the emu campaign, The Argus (Melbourne) · 1932
Emu War · Encyclopaedia Britannica
emu-war.text:
In 1932 the Australian army went to war against emus. The emus won

In 1932 Australian soldiers with machine guns failed to control 20,000 emus; the operation was withdrawn and the emus 'won'.
emu-war.title: The War Australia Lost to Birds

sources: The Secret History of the Mongols · Anonymous, translated by Igor de Rachewiltz · 2004
The Mongols and the Islamic World · Peter Jackson · 2017
Genghis Khan · Encyclopaedia Britannica
genghis-postal.text:
A Mongol message could cross 300 kilometres in a day, faster than any news in Europe until the railway

From 1206 the Mongols built the yam, a relay of horse stations that moved messages 200 to 300 kilometres a day and bound the largest land empire in history together.
genghis-postal.title: The Empire That Ran on Horseback

sources: Early Neolithic wine of Georgia in the South Caucasus, PNAS · Patrick McGovern and others · 2017
Ancient Georgian traditional Qvevri wine-making method · UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage · 2013
Ancient Wine: The Search for the Origins of Viniculture · Patrick E. McGovern · 2003
georgian-wine.text:
The oldest chemical traces of wine on Earth were found in clay jars in the hills south of Tbilisi

Pottery from Neolithic villages in Georgia dated to about 6000 BCE carries the oldest chemical evidence of grape wine, and Georgians still ferment wine in buried clay qvevri today.
georgian-wine.title: Eight Thousand Years of Wine

sources: Commentaries · Pope Pius II · 1460
An odd kind of melancholy: reflections on the glass delusion in Europe (1440–1680), History of Psychiatry · Gill Speak · 1990
Charles VI · Encyclopaedia Britannica
glass-king.text:
A king of France had iron rods sewn into his clothes so that he would not shatter

Charles VI of France suffered episodes from 1392, including the belief that he was made of glass; his incapacity split France and invited English invasion.
glass-king.title: The King Who Believed He Was Made of Glass

sources: Göbekli Tepe: A Stone Age Sanctuary in South-Eastern Anatolia · Klaus Schmidt · 2012
Göbekli Tepe · UNESCO World Heritage Centre
Göbekli Tepe · Encyclopaedia Britannica
gobekli-tepe.text:
Hunter-gatherers raised carved stone pillars 6,000 years before Stonehenge

Göbekli Tepe, built around 9500 BCE by hunter-gatherers, shows that monumental construction came before farming, not after it.
gobekli-tepe.title: The Temple Older Than Farming

sources: Geography, Book XI · Strabo · 20
Vani: An Ancient City of Colchis · Otar Lordkipanidze · 1991
The Jason Voyage: The Quest for the Golden Fleece · Tim Severin · 1985
golden-fleece.text:
The Greek myth of Jason's Golden Fleece may describe a real mining technique used in ancient Georgia

The Golden Fleece myth is set in Colchis, in western Georgia; Strabo linked it to a real practice of catching river gold in sheepskins, a technique used in Svaneti into modern times.
golden-fleece.title: Why Was the Fleece Golden?

sources: The Diary of Samuel Pepys · Samuel Pepys · 1666
By Permission of Heaven: The Story of the Great Fire of London · Adrian Tinniswood · 2003
Great Fire of London · Encyclopaedia Britannica
great-fire-london.text:
Woken to see the blaze, London's mayor said 'a woman might piss it out' and went back to bed

The Great Fire of September 1666 destroyed 13,200 houses and most of old London after the mayor dismissed it; only six deaths were recorded, and the city was rebuilt in brick.
great-fire-london.title: The Fire the Mayor Said Could Be Put Out With Urine

sources: The Great Stink of London: Sir Joseph Bazalgette and the Cleansing of the Victorian Metropolis · Stephen Halliday · 1999
The Ghost Map · Steven Johnson · 2006
Joseph Bazalgette · Encyclopaedia Britannica
great-stink.text:
In 1858 the Thames stank so badly that MPs soaked their curtains in lime and thought of leaving London

In the hot summer of 1858 the stench of the sewage-filled Thames drove Parliament to fund Bazalgette's sewers within eighteen days; the system ended London's cholera and still serves the city.
great-stink.title: The Summer Parliament Fled the Smell

sources: Great Zimbabwe · Peter Garlake · 1973
Great Zimbabwe National Monument · UNESCO World Heritage Centre
Great Zimbabwe · Encyclopaedia Britannica
great-zimbabwe.text:
Colonial rulers banned archaeologists from saying who built Africa's greatest medieval city

Great Zimbabwe, built by Shona ancestors between about 1100 and 1450, was a stone city of up to 18,000 people trading gold across the Indian Ocean; colonial authorities suppressed its African origin for decades.
great-zimbabwe.title: The Stone City Europe Refused to Believe In

sources: Gregorian Reform of the Calendar · G. V. Coyne, M. A. Hoskin and O. Pedersen (editors) · 1983
The Calendar · David Ewing Duncan · 1998
Gregorian calendar · Encyclopaedia Britannica
gregorian-calendar.text:
In 1582 Europeans went to bed on 4 October and woke up on 15 October

In October 1582 Pope Gregory XIII deleted ten days and changed the leap-year rule to fix Caesar's calendar; Protestant and Orthodox countries took up to 340 years to follow.
gregorian-calendar.title: The Ten Days That Never Happened

sources: Gutenberg: How One Man Remade the World with Words · John Man · 2002
The Printing Revolution in Early Modern Europe · Elizabeth L. Eisenstein · 1983
Johannes Gutenberg · Encyclopaedia Britannica
gutenberg-1455.text:
The man who gave Europe printing was sued by his investor and lost his press the year his Bible was finished

Gutenberg's type mould made movable-type printing practical, and his Bible was finished around 1455; that same year his investor Fust won a lawsuit and took the press.
gutenberg-1455.title: The Inventor Who Lost His Invention

sources: Avengers of the New World: The Story of the Haitian Revolution · Laurent Dubois · 2004
The Black Jacobins · C. L. R. James · 1938
Haitian Revolution · Encyclopaedia Britannica
haiti-1804.text:
Enslaved people defeated three empires and founded a nation, then were made to pay for their freedom

Between 1791 and 1804 enslaved people in Saint-Domingue defeated France, Spain and Britain and founded Haiti; in 1825 France extorted an indemnity that Haiti paid until 1947.
haiti-1804.title: The Only Successful Slave Revolution

sources: Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor · Martha T. Roth · 1997
Code of Hammurabi, collection record · Musée du Louvre
Code of Hammurabi · Encyclopaedia Britannica
hammurabi-code.text:
Nearly 4,000 years ago a king set the price of a surgeon's mistake: his hand

Around 1754 BCE Hammurabi of Babylon carved 282 laws on a stone pillar, one of the earliest and most complete legal codes, with penalties that depended on social rank.
hammurabi-code.title: The Laws Carved in Stone

sources: The Histories, Book III · Polybius · -140
Hannibal's War · Livy · 10
Hannibal · Encyclopaedia Britannica
hannibal-alps.text:
A general marched 37 elephants across snowbound mountains to attack Rome from the north

In 218 BCE Hannibal led his army and 37 elephants over the Alps, losing half his men and nearly all the elephants, then crushed Rome at Cannae but never took the city.
hannibal-alps.title: Elephants Over the Alps

sources: The Battle of Hastings 1066 · M. K. Lawson · 2003
The Bayeux Tapestry: A Critically Annotated Bibliography · John F. Szabo and Nicholas E. Kuefler · 2015
Battle of Hastings · Encyclopaedia Britannica
hastings-1066.text:
England's most famous death, an arrow in the king's eye, may be a misreading of a 70-metre embroidery

William of Normandy beat Harold at Hastings in 1066 and took England; the famous arrow in Harold's eye is a later tradition, possibly reinforced by 19th-century restoration of the Bayeux Tapestry.
hastings-1066.title: The Arrow, the Tapestry and the Truth

sources: Greek Thought, Arabic Culture · Dimitri Gutas · 1998
The House of Wisdom: How the Arabs Transformed Western Civilization · Jonathan Lyons · 2009
al-Khwarizmi · Encyclopaedia Britannica
house-of-wisdom.text:
The word 'algorithm' is a mangled version of one Persian scholar's name

Around 820 in Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi wrote the books that carried Indian numerals and systematic algebra to the world; his name became 'algorithm' and his book's title 'algebra'.
house-of-wisdom.title: The Man Who Gave Us Algorithms

sources: The Adventures of Ibn Battuta: A Muslim Traveler of the 14th Century · Ross E. Dunn · 1986
The Travels of Ibn Battuta · translated by H. A. R. Gibb · 1958
Ibn Battuta · Encyclopaedia Britannica
ibn-battuta.text:
A 21-year-old left Morocco for Mecca and came home 29 years and 120,000 kilometres later

Between 1325 and 1354 Ibn Battuta travelled about 120,000 kilometres across Africa and Asia, working as a judge for Muslim rulers, and dictated the Rihla, our richest account of the 14th-century Islamic world.
ibn-battuta.title: The Man Who Travelled Farther Than Marco Polo

sources: Joan of Arc: A History · Helen Castor · 2014
The Trial of Joan of Arc · translated by Daniel Hobbins · 2005
Saint Joan of Arc · Encyclopaedia Britannica
joan-of-arc.text:
A seventeen-year-old farm girl who could not read talked her way into command of an army

In 1429 Joan of Arc, an illiterate teenager, lifted the siege of Orléans in nine days and saw Charles VII crowned; captured and burned in 1431, she was declared innocent in 1456.
joan-of-arc.title: The Teenager Who Turned a War

sources: Krakatoa: The Day the World Exploded · Simon Winchester · 2003
The Eruption of Krakatoa and Subsequent Phenomena · Royal Society Krakatoa Committee · 1888
Krakatoa · Encyclopaedia Britannica
krakatoa-1883.text:
Krakatoa's explosion was heard 4,800 kilometres away and its pressure wave circled the Earth seven times

Krakatoa's eruption on 27 August 1883 produced the loudest sound in recorded history, tsunamis that killed 36,000 and a year of red sunsets; it was the first disaster reported worldwide by telegraph.
krakatoa-1883.title: The Loudest Sound in Recorded History

sources: The Incas · Terence N. D'Altroy · 2002
Signs of the Inka Khipu · Gary Urton · 2003
Machu Picchu: Unveiling the Mystery of the Incas · Richard L. Burger and Lucy C. Salazar · 2004
machu-picchu.text:
The Inca ran an empire of ten million people using knotted strings, and we still cannot fully read them

The Inca ran an empire of millions with knotted khipu, a labour economy and 40,000 kilometres of road; Machu Picchu was a royal estate built around 1450, and the empire fell to Pizarro and smallpox after 1532.
machu-picchu.title: The Empire Without Writing

sources: The First Voyage Around the World · Antonio Pigafetta, translated by Theodore Cachey · 1995
Over the Edge of the World · Laurence Bergreen · 2003
Ferdinand Magellan · Encyclopaedia Britannica
magellan-lost-day.text:
The first crew to sail around the world came home a day behind everyone else's calendar

The Magellan-Elcano expedition of 1519 to 1522 was the first to circle the globe; sailing west, its eighteen survivors found their careful log was one day behind the calendar at home.
magellan-lost-day.title: The Sailors Who Lost a Day

sources: Masalik al-absar fi mamalik al-amsar · Shihab al-Umari · 1340
African Dominion: A New History of Empire in Early and Medieval West Africa · Michael A. Gomez · 2018
Musa I of Mali · Encyclopaedia Britannica
mansa-musa.text:
One king's pilgrimage spending was so extreme that gold lost value in Egypt for years

Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage displayed Mali's gold wealth so lavishly that gold lost value in Cairo for years.
mansa-musa.title: The Man Who Crashed the Price of Gold

sources: The Histories, Book VI · Herodotus · -430
On the Glory of the Athenians · Plutarch · 100
Battle of Marathon · Encyclopaedia Britannica
marathon-490.text:
The marathon race is named after a heroic run that the earliest sources never mention

The Athenians beat Persia at Marathon in 490 BCE; the famous dying messenger is a legend that appears five centuries later, while the real runner Pheidippides ran to Sparta and lived.
marathon-490.title: The Run That Never Happened

sources: Dark Tide: The Great Boston Molasses Flood of 1919 · Stephen Puleo · 2003
Why the Great Molasses Flood Was So Deadly, Scientific American · Erin McCann · 2016
Great Molasses Flood · Encyclopaedia Britannica
molasses-flood.text:
A tank of syrup burst in Boston, and a wave taller than a man swept the streets at 55 km/h

On 15 January 1919 a badly built tank released 8.7 million litres of molasses through Boston's North End, killing 21; the resulting trial set precedents for engineering liability.
molasses-flood.title: The Wave of Molasses

sources: Becoming Mona Lisa · Donald Sassoon · 2001
The theft of the Mona Lisa · Musée du Louvre
Mona Lisa · Encyclopaedia Britannica
mona-lisa-theft.text:
The Mona Lisa became the world's most famous painting because someone stole it

The 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa by Vincenzo Peruggia, and its 1913 recovery, turned a respected painting into the world's most famous artwork.
mona-lisa-theft.title: The Theft That Made the Mona Lisa Famous

sources: Mémoires du général baron Thiébault · Paul Thiébault · 1893
Treaties of Tilsit · Encyclopaedia Britannica
napoleon-rabbits.text:
Napoleon, conqueror of Europe, once retreated from an army of rabbits

In 1807 a rabbit hunt organised for Napoleon went wrong when tame rabbits charged the hunters, a famous anecdote from one general's memoirs.
napoleon-rabbits.title: The Emperor and the Rabbits

sources: Njinga of Angola: Africa's Warrior Queen · Linda M. Heywood · 2017
Istorica descrizione de' tre regni Congo, Matamba et Angola · Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi · 1687
Nzinga · Encyclopaedia Britannica
nzinga.text:
Offered a mat while the Portuguese governor sat on a chair, she sat on a kneeling servant instead

Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba negotiated with the Portuguese as an equal in 1622, ruled from 1624, fought them for nearly forty years and secured a treaty in 1657.
nzinga.title: The Queen Who Made a Governor Her Chair

sources: Ötzi the Iceman · South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology
New genomic insights into the Iceman, Cell Genomics · Ke Wang and others · 2023
Ötzi · Encyclopaedia Britannica
otzi.text:
A 5,300-year-old murder victim was found with his last meal still in his stomach

Ötzi, found in 1991 in Alpine ice, is a 5,300-year-old man killed by an arrow, preserved with his clothes, copper axe and last meal.
otzi.title: The Man in the Ice

sources: Hot mixing: Mechanistic insights into the durability of ancient Roman concrete, Science Advances · Linda Seymour and others · 2023
Phillipsite and Al-tobermorite mineral cements in Roman marine concrete, American Mineralogist · Marie D. Jackson and others · 2017
Pantheon · Encyclopaedia Britannica
pantheon-concrete.text:
Rome's Pantheon has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, and it is 1,900 years old

Roman concrete, made with volcanic ash and lumps of lime, resists seawater and heals its own cracks; the Pantheon's 43-metre dome has stood since about 126 CE.
pantheon-concrete.title: The Concrete That Heals Itself

sources: An Odd Kind of Fame: Stories of Phineas Gage · Malcolm Macmillan · 2000
Recovery from the passage of an iron bar through the head · John M. Harlow · 1868
Phineas Gage · Encyclopaedia Britannica
phineas-gage.text:
A metre-long iron rod blasted through a railway foreman's skull. He survived and changed neuroscience

In 1848 Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his skull; his doctor's reports of changed personality made him the founding case for frontal-lobe science, though later legends exaggerated his decline.
phineas-gage.title: The Man With the Iron Rod Through His Head

sources: We, the Navigators: The Ancient Art of Landfinding in the Pacific · David Lewis · 1972
High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia, PNAS · Janet Wilmshurst and others · 2011
Native American gene flow into Polynesia predating Easter Island settlement, Nature · Alexander Ioannidis and others · 2020
polynesian-navigators.text:
Polynesians crossed the Pacific by the stars, centuries before Europeans dared leave the coast

Between about 1000 and 1280 Polynesian navigators settled Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand using stars, swells and birds; a 1976 voyage without instruments proved the technique.
polynesian-navigators.title: Finding Islands Without Instruments

sources: Letters 6.16 and 6.20 · Pliny the Younger · 107
Pompeii: The Life of a Roman Town · Mary Beard · 2008
Pompeii · Encyclopaedia Britannica
pompeii-79.text:
Bread was still in the ovens when Pompeii vanished under ash for 1,700 years

In 79 CE Vesuvius buried Pompeii; most residents fled during the pumice fall, and those who stayed died in a pyroclastic surge, leaving a town preserved in ash.
pompeii-79.title: The City Frozen in a Day

sources: Edge of Empires: A History of Georgia · Donald Rayfield · 2012
Histories and Eulogies of the Sovereigns · Anonymous Georgian chronicler · 1220
Tamar · Encyclopaedia Britannica
queen-tamar.text:
Georgia's greatest ruler was a woman crowned twice, divorced once, and titled 'King of Kings'

Tamar ruled Georgia from 1184 to 1213 as 'King of Kings', divorced a husband imposed on her, won decisive wars and presided over the golden age celebrated in Rustaveli's epic.
queen-tamar.title: The Queen They Called King

sources: The Radium Girls: The Dark Story of America's Shining Women · Kate Moore · 2016
Deadly Glow: The Radium Dial Worker Tragedy · Ross Mullner · 1999
Radium Girls · Encyclopaedia Britannica
radium-girls.text:
Factory workers were told radium paint was harmless and taught to sharpen their brushes with their lips

From 1917 dial painters were taught to lick radium brushes while their employer hid the danger; their lawsuits in 1928 and 1938 established employer liability for occupational disease.
radium-girls.title: The Women Who Glowed in the Dark

sources: The Lives of the Caesars: Vespasian, 23 · Suetonius · 121
The World of the Fullo · Miko Flohr · 2013
Fulling · Encyclopaedia Britannica
roman-laundry.text:
Ancient Romans washed their clothes in urine, and the emperor taxed it

Roman laundries cleaned wool with ammonia from stale urine, and Vespasian's tax on the trade gave us 'money does not stink'.
roman-laundry.title: Rome's Dirty Little Secret

sources: The Rosetta Stone, collection record · British Museum
Cracking the Egyptian Code · Andrew Robinson · 2012
Rosetta Stone · Encyclopaedia Britannica
rosetta-stone.text:
For 1,400 years nobody on Earth could read hieroglyphs. Then soldiers pulled a slab out of a wall

Found in 1799, the Rosetta Stone's three scripts let Champollion decode hieroglyphs in 1822 and reopen Egypt's written past.
rosetta-stone.title: The Stone That Gave Egypt Its Voice Back

sources: In the Devil's Snare: The Salem Witchcraft Crisis of 1692 · Mary Beth Norton · 2002
Salem Possessed: The Social Origins of Witchcraft · Paul Boyer and Stephen Nissenbaum · 1974
Salem witch trials · Encyclopaedia Britannica
salem-1692.text:
Nineteen people were hanged as witches in Massachusetts because children said they saw ghosts

In 1692 the Salem witch trials hanged nineteen people and pressed one to death on 'spectral evidence' from young accusers; the court stopped only when the governor's wife was named.
salem-1692.title: The Village That Hanged Its Neighbours

sources: The Etiology, Concept, and Prophylaxis of Childbed Fever · Ignaz Semmelweis, translated by K. Codell Carter · 1983
Childbed Fever: A Scientific Biography of Ignaz Semmelweis · K. Codell Carter and Barbara Carter · 1994
Ignaz Semmelweis · Encyclopaedia Britannica
semmelweis.text:
He cut maternal deaths by ninety percent with a bowl of chlorine water, and his colleagues drove him out

In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis cut deaths from childbed fever from about 18 to 1 percent by making doctors wash in chlorine; rejected by his profession, he died in an asylum in 1865, vindicated by germ theory soon after.
semmelweis.title: The Doctor Who Asked Doctors to Wash Their Hands

sources: The Tale of Genji · Murasaki Shikibu, translated by Royall Tyler · 2001
The Diary of Lady Murasaki · Murasaki Shikibu, translated by Richard Bowring · 1996
Murasaki Shikibu · Encyclopaedia Britannica
tale-of-genji.text:
A thousand years ago a Japanese court lady wrote a 1,000-page novel. We don't know her real name

Around 1008 Murasaki Shikibu, a lady of the Heian court whose real name is unknown, wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.
tale-of-genji.title: The First Novel Was Written by a Woman

sources: Tambora: The Eruption That Changed the World · Gillen D'Arcy Wood · 2014
Mount Tambora · Encyclopaedia Britannica
Tambora eruption record · Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program
tambora-1816.text:
In 1816 it snowed in June in New England, and the reason was a volcano on the other side of the world

Tambora's 1815 eruption cooled the planet, causing the failed summer of 1816, famine, and the birth of Frankenstein.
tambora-1816.title: The Year Without a Summer

sources: The True History of the Conquest of New Spain · Bernal Díaz del Castillo · 1568
Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés and the Fall of Old Mexico · Hugh Thomas · 1993
Tenochtitlán · Encyclopaedia Britannica
tenochtitlan-1519.text:
Spanish soldiers who had seen Venice and Rome said they had never seen anything like it

In 1519 the Spanish entered Tenochtitlan, an Aztec lake city of perhaps 200,000 with canals, aqueducts and a vast market, larger than any city in Spain; they destroyed it in 1521.
tenochtitlan-1519.title: The City on the Lake

sources: The Histories, Book VII · Herodotus · -430
Thermopylae: The Battle That Changed the World · Paul Cartledge · 2006
Battle of Thermopylae · Encyclopaedia Britannica
thermopylae-480.text:
Sparta's famous last stand was fought by thousands of Greeks, and the 300 did not fight alone

At Thermopylae in 480 BCE some 7,000 Greeks held a narrow pass for three days; the Spartan 300 and 700 Thespians died covering the retreat, a defeat that became a symbol.
thermopylae-480.title: The 300 Who Were Really 7,000

sources: Zheng He: China and the Oceans in the Early Ming Dynasty · Edward L. Dreyer · 2007
When China Ruled the Seas · Louise Levathes · 1994
Zheng He · Encyclopaedia Britannica
treasure-fleet.text:
Almost a century before Columbus, China sent hundreds of ships across the Indian Ocean. Then it stopped

Between 1405 and 1433 Zheng He's huge Ming fleets reached East Africa, decades before Europe's smaller voyages, and then China chose to stop.
treasure-fleet.title: The Fleet That Dwarfed Columbus

sources: Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age · Anne Goldgar · 2007
Famous First Bubbles · Peter M. Garber · 2000
Tulip Mania · Encyclopaedia Britannica
tulip-mania.text:
In 1637 some Dutch traders paid the price of a canal house for a single tulip bulb

In 1637 Dutch tulip prices spiked to the cost of a house and crashed; the scale of the damage was later exaggerated.
tulip-mania.title: The Flower Worth a House

sources: The Tomb of Tut.ankh.Amen · Howard Carter and A. C. Mace · 1923
Tutankhamun: The Untold Story · Thomas Hoving · 1978
Tutankhamun · Encyclopaedia Britannica
tutankhamun-tomb.text:
The most famous pharaoh was a minor king whose tomb survived only because it was forgotten

Tutankhamun's tomb, found intact by Howard Carter in 1922, survived because debris hid its entrance; it holds the only complete royal burial of ancient Egypt.
tutankhamun-tomb.title: The Boy King Nobody Remembered

sources: The Enemy at the Gate: Habsburgs, Ottomans and the Battle for Europe · Andrew Wheatcroft · 2008
August Zang and the French Croissant · Jim Chevallier · 2009
Siege of Vienna · Encyclopaedia Britannica
vienna-1683.text:
Legend says Vienna's bakers marked the Ottoman defeat with crescents. The pastry is older than the tale

The Ottoman siege of Vienna ended on 12 September 1683 with Sobieski's cavalry charge; the croissant legend attached to it is a 19th-century invention.
vienna-1683.title: Did the Croissant Come From a Siege?

sources: Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021, Nature · Margot Kuitems and others · 2021
L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site · Parks Canada
Vinland · Encyclopaedia Britannica
vinland.text:
Norse sailors were building houses in North America around the year 1000

Norse Greenlanders built a camp at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, dated to 1021 CE, nearly five centuries before Columbus.
vinland.title: The Europeans Who Beat Columbus by 470 Years

sources: Wojtek the Bear: Polish War Hero · Aileen Orr · 2010
Soldier Bear · Geoffrey Morgan and W. A. Lasocki · 1970
Wojtek · Imperial War Museums
wojtek-bear.text:
A Syrian brown bear was formally enlisted in the Polish army so he could board a troopship to Italy

Wojtek, a bear cub adopted by Polish soldiers in Iran in 1942, was enlisted as a private, reportedly carried shells at Monte Cassino, and lived out his life at Edinburgh Zoo until 1963.
wojtek-bear.title: The Bear Who Was a Private

sources: Wu Zhao: China's Only Woman Emperor · N. Harry Rothschild · 2008
The Cambridge History of China, vol. 3 · Denis Twitchett (editor) · 1979
Wuhou · Encyclopaedia Britannica
wu-zetian.text:
A concubine's daughter founded her own dynasty and invented new Chinese characters, one for her name

Wu Zetian, a former concubine, ruled China as emperor of her own Zhou dynasty from 690 to 705, the only woman ever to hold the title.
wu-zetian.title: The Only Woman to Rule China as Emperor

sources: Alpine ice-core evidence for the transformation of the European monetary system, AD 640–670, Antiquity · Christopher Loveluck and others · 2018
Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age, Nature Geoscience · Ulf Büntgen and others · 2016
History of the Wars, Book IV · Procopius · 550
year-536.text:
In 536 the sun went dim for eighteen months and summer snow fell in China

In 536 CE an Icelandic eruption dimmed the sun for over a year, beginning the coldest decade in two millennia, followed by famine and Justinian's plague in 541.
year-536.title: The Worst Year to Be Alive

sources: Britain's Forgotten Wars · Ian Hernon · 2003
Anglo-Zanzibar War · Encyclopaedia Britannica
Shortest war: Guinness World Records
zanzibar-war.text:
The shortest war in history was over before breakfast went cold

In 1896 a succession dispute in Zanzibar ended after roughly 40 minutes of British naval bombardment, the shortest war on record.
zanzibar-war.title: The War That Lasted 40 Minutes
